**Rushanara Ali** ([/ˌ r uː ʃ ə ˈ n ɑːr ə ə ˈ l iː/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language "Bengali language"): রুশনারা আলী, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Bengali "Romanization of Bengali"):_Ruśnara Ali_, IPA:[[ˈɾuʃnaˌɾa‿ˈali]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali "Help:IPA/Bengali"); born 14 March 1975) is a British politician who has served as a [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") since 2010 and as [Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under-Secretary_of_State_for_Homelessness_and_Democracy "Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) from July 2024 to August 2025.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-home-1)

Ali was elected to represent [Bethnal Green and Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethnal_Green_and_Bow "Bethnal Green and Bow") in 2010 as a member of [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") and represented the constituency until its abolition in 2024. She currently represents the [Bethnal Green and Stepney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethnal_Green_and_Stepney "Bethnal Green and Stepney") constituency, having won it in the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Ali was born on 14 March 1975 in [Bishwanath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishwanath "Bishwanath"), [Sylhet District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylhet_District "Sylhet District"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews241-4) With her family, Ali emigrated to the [East End of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_of_London "East End of London") at the age of seven, where she attended [Mulberry School for Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulberry_School_for_Girls "Mulberry School for Girls") and [Tower Hamlets College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hamlets_College "Tower Hamlets College"). She grew up in [Tower Hamlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hamlets "Tower Hamlets"), and was the first in her family to go to university, reading [PPE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_politics_and_economics "Philosophy, politics and economics") at [St John's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Oxford "St John's College, Oxford").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-sjc-bio-5)

## Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early career")]

Ali began her career as a research assistant to [Michael Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Young,_Baron_Young_of_Dartington "Michael Young, Baron Young of Dartington"), working on a project which paved the way for the establishment of [Tower Hamlets Summer University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hamlets_Summer_University "Tower Hamlets Summer University"), offering independent learning programmes for young people aged 11–25. She helped to develop "[Language Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_Line "Language Line")", a national telephone interpreting service in over 100 languages. Between 1997 and 1999 she was parliamentary assistant to [Oona King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oona_King "Oona King"), MP for Bethnal Green and Bow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-rushanaraali--6)

Ali worked on human rights issues at the [Foreign Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Office "Foreign Office") from 2000 to 2001. Prior to this, she was a research fellow at the [Institute of Public Policy Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Public_Policy_Research "Institute of Public Policy Research") (IPPR) focussing on anti-discrimination issues from 1999 to 2002. From 2002 to 2005, she worked in the community cohesion unit at the Communities Directorate of the [Home Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Office "Home Office"), leading a work programme to mobilise local and national agencies in the aftermath of the 2001 riots in [Burnley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnley "Burnley"), [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Bradford_riots "2001 Bradford riots") and [Oldham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Oldham_riots "2001 Oldham riots"), to prevent further conflict and unrest, challenging central Government to provide appropriate support to these areas.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbwhoswho08-7)

Previously, Ali worked as associate director of the [Young Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Foundation "Young Foundation") in [Bethnal Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethnal_Green "Bethnal Green"), a [thinktank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinktank "Thinktank") focused on [social innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_innovation "Social innovation"). She has also served as Chair of [Tower Hamlets Summer University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hamlets_Summer_University "Tower Hamlets Summer University"); a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of [Tower Hamlets College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hamlets_College "Tower Hamlets College"); Trustee of the [Paul Hamlyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hamlyn "Paul Hamlyn") Foundation; and member of the [Tate Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Britain "Tate Britain") Council.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-socialinnovationexchange-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)

Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_, _[Prospect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospect\_(magazine) "Prospect (magazine)")_ magazine and _[Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress\_(organisation) "Progress (organisation)")_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on [Question Time Extra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Question_Time_(TV_series) "Question Time (TV series)"), [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4")'s _Woman's Hour_ and _[Thinking Allowed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking\_Allowed "Thinking Allowed")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)

In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

## Parliamentary career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Parliamentary career")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Rushanara_Ali.jpg/250px-Rushanara_Ali.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rushanara_Ali.jpg)

Ali at the Forum Libération de [Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble "Grenoble") in February 2013

In April 2007, Ali was chosen as the Labour Party's [prospective Parliamentary candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospective_Parliamentary_candidate "Prospective Parliamentary candidate") for Bethnal Green and Bow. In [May 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election"), she was elected as a Member of Parliament with a majority of 11,574 votes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-eastlondonadvertiser1-17) She is the first person of Bangladeshi origin to have been elected to the House of Commons,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-thisislondon-18) and along with [Shabana Mahmood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabana_Mahmood "Shabana Mahmood") and [Yasmin Qureshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasmin_Qureshi "Yasmin Qureshi"), became one of the United Kingdom's first female Muslim MPs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian3-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-20)

In February 2013, Ali voted in favour of the [Same Sex Marriage Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Same_Sex_Couples)_Act_2013 "Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-auto-21) This drew support from pro-[LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") activists such as [Peter Tatchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Tatchell "Peter Tatchell"), but condemnation from religious figures such as the [imams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imam "Imam") of mosques in [Tooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooting "Tooting") and [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford "Bradford").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-auto-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-22) She would later defend a constituent who alleged he was a victim of [homophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobic "Homophobic")[hate crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crime "Hate crime") after his neighbours sang songs at him with the words "queer", "fairy" and "fag", calling for the case to be reconsidered in a letter to the [Crown Prosecution Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prosecution_Service "Crown Prosecution Service").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-23)

In April 2013, Ali was appointed a Governor of the UK government-funded [Westminster Foundation for Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Foundation_for_Democracy "Westminster Foundation for Democracy").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-wfd-governors-24)

Ali served as Shadow Minister of State for International Development from October 2010 to October 2013.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-25) In the October 2013 Labour frontbench reshuffle, Ali was appointed Shadow Minister of State for Education.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-labourlist-26)

On 26 September 2014, she resigned from the Shadow Education team to abstain on the [Coalition government's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Clegg_coalition "Cameron–Clegg coalition") House of Commons motion permitting military action against [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") in Iraq.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc3-27)

Ali also told Miliband that she remained totally committed to his leadership and was looking forward to his becoming the prime minister in next eight months' time. In his return letter to Ali, Miliband praised her as 'someone with great ability and talent'. Regretting her departure from the frontbench team, the Labour leader added that he accepted the resignation with due respect to her decision.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-thetimes-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews242-29)

Ali retained her seat at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), with a 61% share of the vote and her majority doubling to 24,317.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-30) In June 2015, she was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") as a candidate in the [Labour leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-newstatesman-31) Ali announced she would stand in the [2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2015 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), but withdrew just before the nominations deadline.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-32)

In April 2016, British Prime Minister [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") appointed Ali as the [Prime Ministerial Trade Envoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Ministerial_Trade_Envoy "Prime Ministerial Trade Envoy") to [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews243-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-dhakatribune-34) as part of cross-party trade envoy network.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prothom-alo-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-newsnextbd-36) She supported [Owen Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Smith "Owen Smith") in the failed attempt to replace [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") in the [2016 leadership Election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), calling on Corbyn to "do the decent thing" and quit as Labour leader.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-38)

Ali campaigned to remain in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") in the [2016 membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum") and in 2017 voted against the triggering of Article 50.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-39)

In June 2017, in the [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), Ali retained her seat with an increased majority of 35,393.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc4-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-standard-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-eastlondonadvertiser2-42)

In March 2018, Ali received a suspicious package containing an [anti-Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia "Islamophobia") letter and sticky liquid.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-eastlondonadvertiser3-43) The substance was later found to be harmless. Similar packages were received by fellow Labour MPs [Mohammad Yasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Yasin_(politician) "Mohammad Yasin (politician)"), [Rupa Huq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupa_Huq "Rupa Huq") and [Afzal Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afzal_Khan_(British_politician) "Afzal Khan (British politician)").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-theguardian-45)

In October 2018, Ali signed the 'MPs not border guards' pledge, committing to not report constituents to the [Home Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Office "Home Office") for immigration enforcement.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-46)

As of 2019, Ali is part of the executive committee of the [British-American Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British-American_Project "British-American Project").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bap-ukexec-47) In December 2019, in the [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), Ali retained her seat with an increased majority of 37,524.

In early 2020, Ali supported [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer") in the 2020 Labour Party leadership election.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-48)

In March 2020, Ali was one of 76 Labour MPs to urge that the government grant recourse to public funds for all migrants in the UK regardless of their legal status.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-49)

In March 2021, a 42-year-old man was sentenced after orchestrating an 18-month hate campaign against Ali which included death threats.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-50)

In November 2022, as a serving MP, Ali received £10,000 for 32 hours of work to represent a privately funded "Commission of Inquiry" to investigate the [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") Government and the detention of Zhanbolat Mamay.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-51) In a press conference on 20 January 2023, Bindmans LLP, the project manager, refused to disclose the name of their client but revealed it was a Kazakhstan citizen or citizens.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-52)

In the [September 2023 British shadow cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_British_shadow_cabinet_reshuffle "2023 British shadow cabinet reshuffle"), she was appointed [Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under-Secretary_of_State_for_Enterprise,_Markets_and_Small_Business "Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Enterprise, Markets and Small Business").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-53)

During the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"), Ali faced significant criticism from some constituents for following the Labour Party whip and abstaining on the SNP’s ceasefire motion.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-Butt_2023-11-15-54) Ali had previously called for a humanitarian ceasefire and continued to call for a ceasefire into 2024.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-56)

Ali is a member of [Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Friends_of_Palestine_and_the_Middle_East "Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-r765-57)

During the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"), she saw her 37,000-majority reduced to 1,700, and thus only narrowly avoided losing her seat to independent candidate [Ajmal Masroor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajmal_Masroor "Ajmal Masroor").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-58) Death threats and voter intimidation left Ali needing police protection during her re-election campaign.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-59)

### Ministerial career (2024–2025)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ministerial career (2024–2025)")]

Following Labour's victory in the 2024 general election, Ali was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Building Safety and Homelessness in the [Starmer ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starmer_ministry "Starmer ministry").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-61)

On 19 October 2024, Ali relinquished her portfolio of Building Safety after survivors of the [Grenfell Tower fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenfell_Tower_fire "Grenfell Tower fire") called for her resignation due to Ali previously attending a conference sponsored by [Saint-Gobain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gobain "Saint-Gobain"), one of the firms heavily criticised in the [Grenfell Tower Inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenfell_Tower_Inquiry "Grenfell Tower Inquiry"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) when serving as Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business. She retained her ministerial role in the department with responsibility for homelessness and rough sleeping, as well as taking on the role as Minister for Democracy.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-63)

#### Resignation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Resignation")]

On 7 August 2025, she faced strong criticism after it had been reported that she evicted tenants from her property in [Bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow,_London "Bow, London") whilst serving as the minister for homelessness, but a few weeks later raised rent prices after failing to resell the property. Ali's letting agencies also attempted to charge tenants for repainting and professional cleaning, contrary to the [Tenant Fees Act 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenant_Fees_Act_2019 "Tenant Fees Act 2019").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-inews-20250806-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian-20250807-65) Ali had introduced the [Renters' Rights Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renters'_Rights_Act_2025 "Renters' Rights Act 2025") to ban landlords from relisting vacant properties at higher rates, prompting accusations of hypocrisy.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian-20250807-65) She resigned the same day.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) In her resignation letter, Ali claimed there was no wrongdoing but stated she had become a "distraction" for the government.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-66)

### Post-Ministerial career (since 2025)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rushanara_Ali&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-Ministerial career (since 2025)")]

In March 2026, Ali joined MPs calling for a ban on political donations in cryptocurrency, citing "the threat of foreign interference in our democracy".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-67)

**Margaret Mary Beckett, Baroness Beckett** (_[née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth\_name#Maiden\_and\_married\_names "Birth name")_**Jackson**; born 15 January 1943) is a British politician who was the United Kingdom's first female [Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Secretary_(United_Kingdom) "Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)") (from 2006 to 2007) and a [member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for more than 45 years, first from 1974 to 1979 and then from 1983 to 2024. A member of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"), she was and served as a minister under Prime Ministers [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson"), [James Callaghan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Callaghan "James Callaghan"), [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") and [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown"). Beckett was [Deputy Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Opposition "Deputy Leader of the Opposition") and [Deputy Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") from 1992 to 1994, and briefly [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom) "Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)") and acting [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") following [John Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smith_(Labour_Party_leader) "John Smith (Labour Party leader)")'s death in 1994. A member of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)"), she served as MP for [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_(constituency) "Lincoln (constituency)") from 1974 to 1979, and for [Derby South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South "Derby South") from 1983 to 2024. Her 45 years in the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") makes her the female MP in the Commons with the longest service overall ([Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman") has longer continuous service), and she was the last sitting MP who served in the Labour governments of the 1970s.

Beckett was first elected to [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") at the [October 1974 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_1974_United_Kingdom_general_election "October 1974 United Kingdom general election") for Lincoln and held junior positions in the governments of Harold Wilson and James Callaghan. She lost her seat at the [1979 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_United_Kingdom_general_election "1979 United Kingdom general election"), but returned to the Commons in 1983 as MP for Derby South. She was appointed to [Neil Kinnock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Kinnock "Neil Kinnock")'s [shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinnock_shadow_cabinet "Kinnock shadow cabinet") shortly afterwards; she was elected Deputy Leader of the Labour Party in 1992, becoming the first woman to hold that role. When [John Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smith_(Labour_Party_leader) "John Smith (Labour Party leader)") died in 1994, Beckett became the first woman to lead the Labour Party, though only in a temporary capacity—Blair won the [election to replace Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Labour_Party_leadership_election "1994 Labour Party leadership election") shortly afterward and assumed the substantive leadership.

After Labour returned to power in 1997, and as one of [101 female Labour MPs elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blair_Babes "Blair Babes"), Beckett became a member of Blair's [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Kingdom "Cabinet of the United Kingdom") initially as [President of the Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Board_of_Trade "President of the Board of Trade"), the first female holder of that office. She later served as [Leader of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_House_of_Commons "Leader of the House of Commons") and [Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs"), before becoming Foreign Secretary in 2006, the first woman to hold that position, and—after [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")—the second woman to hold one of the [Great Offices of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Offices_of_State "Great Offices of State"). Following Blair's resignation as [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") in 2007, Beckett was not initially given a position by Brown, Blair's successor; after she had spent a period on the backbenches, Brown appointed her to his cabinet as [Minister of State for Housing and Planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_State_for_Housing_and_Planning "Minister of State for Housing and Planning") in 2008, before she left the government for the last time in 2009. After Labour lost power following the [2010 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election"), she sat on the opposition backbenches until standing down at the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"). She was shortly thereafter appointed to the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Margaret Beckett was born Margaret Mary Jackson in 1943, in [Ashton-under-Lyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton-under-Lyne "Ashton-under-Lyne"), Lancashire, into the family of a disabled Congregationalist carpenter father and an Irish Catholic teacher mother. Her father died early, precipitating family [poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty "Poverty").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-3) She had two sisters, one later a nun, the other later a doctor and mother of three. She was educated at the [Notre Dame High School for Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_High_School,_Norwich "Notre Dame High School, Norwich") in [Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich "Norwich"), then at [University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester_Institute_of_Science_and_Technology "University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology"), where she took a degree in [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Telegraph_educ-4)

Beckett was an active member of the Students' Union and served on its council. In 1961, she joined [Associated Electrical Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Electrical_Industries "Associated Electrical Industries") as a student apprentice in metallurgy. She also joined the [Transport and General Workers Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_and_General_Workers_Union "Transport and General Workers Union") in 1964. In 1966, she joined the [University of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester "University of Manchester") as an experiment officer in its metallurgy department, and in 1970 went to work for the Labour Party as a researcher in [industrial policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_policy "Industrial policy").

## Member of Parliament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Member of Parliament")]

In 1973, Beckett was selected as Labour candidate for [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_(constituency) "Lincoln (constituency)"), which the party wanted to win back from ex-Labour MP [Dick Taverne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Taverne "Dick Taverne"), who had won the [Lincoln by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Lincoln_by-election "1973 Lincoln by-election") in March 1973 standing as the [Democratic Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Labour_Party_(UK,_1972) "Democratic Labour Party (UK, 1972)") candidate. At the [February 1974 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_1974_United_Kingdom_general_election "February 1974 United Kingdom general election"), Beckett lost to Taverne by 1,297 votes. Following the election, she worked as a researcher for [Judith Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Hart "Judith Hart"), the [Minister for Overseas Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Overseas_Development "Minister for Overseas Development") at the Foreign Office. [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") called the [October 1974 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_1974_United_Kingdom_general_election "October 1974 United Kingdom general election"), and Beckett again stood against Taverne in Lincoln. This time Beckett became the MP, with a majority of 984 votes. Almost immediately following her election she was appointed as [Judith Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Hart "Judith Hart")'s [Parliamentary private secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_private_secretary "Parliamentary private secretary"). [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") made her a [Whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whip_(politics) "Whip (politics)") in 1975,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-5) promoted to [Parliamentary under-secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_under-secretary_of_state "Parliamentary under-secretary of state") at the [Department of Education and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Education_and_Skills_(England) "Department for Education and Skills (England)"), replacing [Joan Lestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Lestor "Joan Lestor"), who had resigned in protest over spending cuts.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-6)

Beckett remained in that position until she lost her seat at the [1979 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_United_Kingdom_general_election "1979 United Kingdom general election"). The [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") candidate [Kenneth Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carlisle "Kenneth Carlisle") narrowly won the seat with a 602-vote majority, the first time the Conservatives had won at Lincoln since [1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_United_Kingdom_general_election "1935 United Kingdom general election"). She joined [Granada Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Television "Granada Television") as a researcher in 1979. Out of Parliament, and now known as Margaret Beckett after her marriage, she was elected to Labour's [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)") in 1980, and supported the left-winger [Tony Benn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Benn "Tony Benn") in the [1981 Labour deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Labour_deputy_leadership_election "1981 Labour deputy leadership election") narrowly won by [Denis Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Healey "Denis Healey"). She was the subject of a vociferous attack by [Joan Lestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Lestor "Joan Lestor") at the conference. Beckett was selected to stand at the [1983 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_United_Kingdom_general_election "1983 United Kingdom general election") as the Labour candidate in the parliamentary constituency of [Derby South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South "Derby South") following the retirement of the sitting MP, [Walter Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Johnson_(politician) "Walter Johnson (politician)"). At the election she retained the seat with a small majority of 421 votes. In March 2022, Beckett announced she would end her parliamentary career, standing down as MP for Derby South at the next general election.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-7)

### Shadow Cabinet and Deputy Leader, 1984–1994

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Shadow Cabinet and Deputy Leader, 1984–1994")]

See also: [Beckett shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckett_shadow_cabinet "Beckett shadow cabinet")

Upon returning to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"), Beckett gradually moved away from the [left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics"), supporting incumbent leader [Neil Kinnock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Kinnock "Neil Kinnock") against Benn in 1988. By this time she was a front bencher, as a spokeswoman on Social Security since 1984, becoming a member of the [shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_cabinet "Shadow cabinet") in 1989 as [Shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Chief_Secretary_to_the_Treasury "Shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury"). Following the [1992 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_Kingdom_general_election "1992 United Kingdom general election") she was elected [Deputy Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") and served under [John Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smith_(Labour_Party_leader) "John Smith (Labour Party leader)") as [Shadow Leader of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Leader_of_the_House_of_Commons "Shadow Leader of the House of Commons"). She became a [Member of the Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_(United_Kingdom) "Privy Council (United Kingdom)") in 1993. She was the first woman to serve as deputy leader of the Labour Party.

Following the sudden death of [John Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smith_(Labour_Party_leader) "John Smith (Labour Party leader)") from a heart attack on 12 May 1994, Beckett became Acting Leader of the Labour Party, the party's constitution providing for the automatic succession of the deputy leader for the remainder of the leadership term, upon the death or resignation of an incumbent leader in opposition. In times when the party is in opposition, party leaders are subject to annual reelection at the time of the annual party conference; accordingly, Beckett was constitutionally entitled to remain in office as acting leader until the 1994 Conference; however, the party's National Executive Committee (NEC) rapidly decided to bring forward the election for Labour Leader and Deputy Leader to July 1994.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-BBC_12_May_04-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-LabourList_19_Aug_21-9)

Beckett decided to run for the position of Labour Leader, but came last in [1994 leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Labour_Party_leadership_election "1994 Labour Party leadership election"), behind [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") and [John Prescott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Prescott "John Prescott"). The deputy leadership was contested at the same time; Beckett was also defeated in this contest, coming second behind Prescott. Though she failed in both contests, she was retained in the shadow cabinet by Blair as [Shadow Health Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Health_Secretary "Shadow Health Secretary").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-LabourList_19_Aug_21-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Guardian_22_Jul_94-10)

A footnote to her ten-week tenure as caretaker leader of the Labour Party is that she was the leader at the time of the [1994 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "1994 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom"), which were held four weeks after she assumed the position. Labour's election campaign had been long in the planning under Smith, whose sudden death led to a "sympathy rise" in opinion polls for Labour, compounding what had already been a strong lead over the Conservatives. Consequently, Labour had a commanding victory in what was its best result in any of the four European elections held since 1979. The two Labour leadership elections followed six weeks later on 21 July 1994 and the Labour electorate did not appear to attribute any credit for the successful European election result to Beckett's chance-ordained position as acting leader in the four weeks immediately prior to the election.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Under Blair's leadership, Beckett was the Shadow Secretary of State for [Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Health_and_Social_Care "Department of Health and Social Care"), and then from 1995 the [Shadow President of the Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_President_of_the_Board_of_Trade "Shadow President of the Board of Trade"). She was one of the leading critics of the government when the [Scott Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Report "Scott Report") published its findings into the [Arms-to-Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms-to-Iraq "Arms-to-Iraq") scandal in 1996.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In [2025 Labour Party deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2025 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), Beckett recalled that being deputy leader was a "ghastly job".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-11)

### In government, 1997–2001

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In government, 1997–2001")]

The Labour Party was elected to government in a [landslide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") in the [1997 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election "1997 United Kingdom general election") and Beckett held a number of senior positions in the [Blair government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Blair_ministry "First Blair ministry"). Following the election she was appointed [President of the Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Board_of_Trade "President of the Board of Trade") (a position whose title later reverted to [Secretary of State for Trade and Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Trade_and_Industry "Secretary of State for Trade and Industry")); the first woman to have held the post. She was succeeded by [Peter Mandelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Mandelson "Peter Mandelson") in July 1998.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Beckett was then [Leader of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_House_of_Commons "Leader of the House of Commons") from 1998 until her replacement by [Robin Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Cook "Robin Cook") in June 2001. Her tenure saw the introduction of [Westminster Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Hall "Westminster Hall") debates, which are debates held in a small chamber near Westminster Hall on topics of interest to individual MPs, committee reports, and other matters that would not ordinarily be debated in the Commons chamber.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-12) Debates that take place in Westminster Hall are often more consensual and informal, and can address the concerns of [backbenchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbencher "Backbencher"). She received admiration for her work as Leader of the House,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-MargProf-13) working on this and a number of other elements of the Labour government's modernisation agenda for Parliament. In 2000, she expressed republican sympathies.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-14)

### Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2001–2006

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2001–2006")]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4e/Official_portrait_of_Margaret_Beckett_as_Environment_Secretary.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_portrait_of_Margaret_Beckett_as_Environment_Secretary.jpg)

Beckett as [Environment Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs")

Following the [2001 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election "2001 United Kingdom general election"), Beckett became Secretary of State at the new [Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_the_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs") (DEFRA), created after the [Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Agriculture,_Fisheries_and_Food_(United_Kingdom) "Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (United Kingdom)") (MAFF) was abolished in the wake of perceived mismanagement of the [foot-and-mouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot-and-mouth "Foot-and-mouth")[epidemic in 2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_foot-and-mouth_outbreak "2001 United Kingdom foot-and-mouth outbreak"). The new department also incorporated some of the functions of the former [Department for the Environment, Transport and the Regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_the_Environment,_Transport_and_the_Regions "Department for the Environment, Transport and the Regions") (DETR).

Beckett rejected demands for an expansion of [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_in_the_United_Kingdom "Nuclear power in the United Kingdom") from a lobby including energy minister [Brian Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Wilson_(Labour_politician) "Brian Wilson (Labour politician)") and Downing Street staff. She argued there was no need for new nuclear for at least 15 years given current energy prices and generation capacity. The 2003 energy [white paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_paper "White paper") stated that "the current economics of nuclear power make it unattractive" and there were no proposals for new nuclear power stations.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-guardian-20040919-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-telegraph-20050508-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-bower-2016-17)

Beckett held the position of [Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs") until May 2006, when she was succeeded by [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"). Beckett was on the front line of the government's efforts to tackle [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), and attended international conferences on the matter.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In a report published on 29 March 2007 by the [Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs_Select_Committee "Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee"), she was criticised for her role in the failures of the [Rural Payments Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_Payments_Agency "Rural Payments Agency") when she had been [Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-18)

### Foreign Secretary: 2006–2007

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Foreign Secretary: 2006–2007")]

Following the [2006 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2006 United Kingdom local elections"), Blair demoted [Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Secretary_(United_Kingdom) "Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)")[Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw"), and appointed Beckett as Straw's successor. She was the first woman to hold the post, and only the second woman (after [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")) to hold one of the [Great Offices of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Offices_of_State "Great Offices of State").

Some commentators claim that Beckett was promoted to Foreign Secretary because she was considered to be a 'safe pair of hands' and a loyal member of the Cabinet.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-20) Her experience at DEFRA in dealing with international climate change issues has also been cited as a factor in the move.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Beckett had to adapt quickly to her diplomatic role; within a few hours of her appointment as Foreign Secretary, she flew to the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") in New York City for an urgent meeting of foreign ministers to discuss the [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") nuclear weapons crisis. About a month later, she came under fire for not responding quickly enough to the [2006 Lebanon War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Lebanon_War "2006 Lebanon War") which saw [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") invade that country, although some reports suggested that the delay was caused by Cabinet division rather than Beckett's reluctance to make a public statement on the matter.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-21)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Beckett_Rice.jpg/250px-Beckett_Rice.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beckett_Rice.jpg)

Beckett appears with [US Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Secretary_of_State "US Secretary of State"), [Condoleezza Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condoleezza_Rice "Condoleezza Rice"), following her appointment as Foreign Secretary

Beckett is understood[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] to have delegated European issues to the [Foreign Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Office "Foreign Office") minister responsible for Europe, [Geoff Hoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Hoon "Geoff Hoon"), who, following his demotion as Defence Secretary, continued to attend Cabinet meetings. Hoon and Beckett were said to have a difficult ministerial relationship.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-22)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-23) As Foreign Secretary, Beckett came in for some trenchant criticism. According to _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_, she did not stand up well in comparison with the previous Foreign Secretary, [Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-24)_[The Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Spectator "The Spectator")_ described her as "at heart, an old, isolationist, pacifist Leftist" and called on her to resign,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-25) and the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ accused her of allowing the Foreign Office to become subservient to 10 Downing Street after the tenures of Straw and [Robin Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Cook "Robin Cook").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-26)

In August 2006, 37 Labour Party members in her Derby South constituency left the party and joined the [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)"), criticising her approach to the [Israeli invasion of Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Lebanon_War "2006 Lebanon War").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-27) Two weeks earlier, Beckett's successor, [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband"), raised concerns during a cabinet meeting about the failure of Blair and Beckett to call for an immediate ceasefire.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-no10rebuff-28) Straw and [Hilary Benn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Benn "Hilary Benn"), then [International Development Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Development_Secretary "International Development Secretary"), also raised concerns. Former minister [Michael Meacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Meacher "Michael Meacher") said there was "despair, anger and bewilderment" in the Labour Party at the UK's failure to call for an immediate ceasefire.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-no10rebuff-28)

### Post-Blair years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Post-Blair years")]

Upon taking office as prime minister, [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown") made it known that Beckett would not continue as foreign secretary.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-29) On 28 June 2007, Brown selected David Miliband as her replacement[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-30) and Beckett returned to the back benches. It was announced on 29 January 2008 that Beckett would become the new head of the Prime Minister's [Intelligence and Security Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_and_Security_Committee "Intelligence and Security Committee"), replacing [Paul Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Murphy,_Baron_Murphy_of_Torfaen "Paul Murphy, Baron Murphy of Torfaen"), who became the [Secretary of State for Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Wales "Secretary of State for Wales").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-31)

Having been tipped for a possible return to the front bench in July 2008, due to her reputation as a solid media performer,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-32) Beckett returned to government in the [reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reshuffle "Reshuffle") on 3 October 2008 as the [Minister of State for Housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_State_for_Housing "Minister of State for Housing") in the [Department for Communities and Local Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Communities_and_Local_Government "Department for Communities and Local Government"). She attended Cabinet meetings, but was not a full member and was not to be entitled to vote on collective decisions. She ultimately was allowed to return due to her cabinet experience and her economic management in the past.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Beckett was a member of the [Top Level Group of UK Parliamentarians for Multilateral Nuclear Disarmament and Non-proliferation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Level_Group "Top Level Group"), established in October 2009.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-33) She has served as a member of the [Henry Jackson Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Jackson_Society "Henry Jackson Society") Advisory Council.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-guardian-20130520-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-hjs-20160808-35)

### Expenses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Expenses")]

Main article: [United Kingdom parliamentary expenses scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_parliamentary_expenses_scandal "United Kingdom parliamentary expenses scandal")

Beckett was found to have claimed £600 for [hanging baskets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_basket "Hanging basket") and [pot plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pot_plant "Pot plant") by _[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ in the [2009 expenses scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_expenses_scandal "2009 expenses scandal"). As she had no [mortgage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage "Mortgage") or [rent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renting "Renting") outstanding it was queried how she managed to claim £72,537 between 2004 and 2008 on a house in her constituency when she was renting out her London flat and living in a [grace and favour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_and_favour "Grace and favour") flat.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-36)

### Bid to become Speaker

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bid to become Speaker")]

On 10 June 2009, Beckett announced that she wished to replace [Michael Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Martin,_Baron_Martin_of_Springburn "Michael Martin, Baron Martin of Springburn") as [Speaker of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_(United_Kingdom) "Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)"). She said: "I think at the moment we have got very considerable problems in Parliament. We have got to make changes.... After the next election, if we have a more finely balanced chamber than we have had in the recent past, it will be a very different ball game.... I hope I can help us deal with that." Beckett received 74 votes in the first round and 70 votes in the second round of the 2009 Speaker election, reaching the third place as the strongest Labour candidate both times but considerably trailing the two Conservative frontrunners [John Bercow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bercow "John Bercow") and [George Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Young,_Baron_Young_of_Cookham "George Young, Baron Young of Cookham"). She withdrew following the second round of voting.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-37) In August 2009, Beckett wrote to Sir Christopher Kelly, Chairman of the [Committee on Standards in Public Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_on_Standards_in_Public_Life "Committee on Standards in Public Life") which was investigating MPs' expenses. In the letter, she says the allowances do not adequately cover MPs' costs, which include political campaigns. _The Telegraph_ criticised the "self-pitying" letter, saying it will fuel "concern that some MPs are not genuinely committed to reform".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-38)

### Alternative Vote referendum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Alternative Vote referendum")]

On 26 November 2010, Beckett was announced as the President of the [NOtoAV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOtoAV "NOtoAV") campaign, which campaigned to retain the [First Past the Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Past_the_Post "First Past the Post") (FPTP) electoral system at the [2011 United Kingdom Alternative Vote referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_United_Kingdom_Alternative_Vote_referendum "2011 United Kingdom Alternative Vote referendum").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-39) She led the campaign to success, and FPTP remains the system used in UK parliamentary elections.

### 2015 Labour leadership election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2015 Labour leadership election")]

Beckett was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") as a candidate in the [Labour leadership election of 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-40) Later, during an interview with [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4")'s _The [World at One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_at\_One "World at One")_, after it became known he was in the lead among the candidates, Beckett was asked if she was "a moron" for nominating Corbyn. She replied: "I am one of them."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-41) In January 2016, Beckett claimed that Labour would need an "unexpected political miracle" if it were to win under his leadership,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-42) and criticised Corbyn for failing to win back the trust of the electorate on [welfare reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_reform "Welfare reform") and [mass immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_immigration "Mass immigration"), saying: "I think we had the right policies towards immigration, but the simple thuggishness of the kind of Ukip and Conservative approach is easier to understand and we didn't overcome those communication difficulties ... We have to try and work on ways to overcome that – I'm not suggesting we've done it yet".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-43) She later supported [Owen Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Smith "Owen Smith") in the failed attempt to replace Corbyn in the [2016 Labour leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-44) In February 2019, she acknowledged during an interview with [Sophy Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophy_Ridge "Sophy Ridge") on [Sky News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_News "Sky News") that she was "surprised" about how Corbyn had "grown into the job" after taking on the leadership. She further claimed that veteran Conservative MP [Kenneth Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Clarke "Kenneth Clarke") called Corbyn a "perfectly competent" opposition leader.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Bartlett_2019-45)

### Beckett report

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Beckett report")]

On 16 January 2016, Beckett released "Learning the Lessons from Defeat Taskforce Report", a 35-page report into why the Labour Party lost the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election") after the then deputy leader [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman") requested Beckett investigate the reasons for Labour's failure.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-46) Labour's defeat came as a shock to pollsters, whose polls had suggested that the result would be much closer than it eventually was. Ultimately, the Conservatives won a narrow majority.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Beckett_Report-47)

The report said that explanations including Labour being "anti-business" or "anti-aspiration" were not "significant" factors, saying that "reasons for defeat should be treated with caution and require deeper analysis".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Beckett_Report-47) The main reasons given for Labour's losses were the perceived weakness of [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") as party leader, fear of Labour's relationship with the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) among English voters, a perceived association with [the financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") under the [Brown ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_ministry "Brown ministry"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Beckett_Report-47) and "issues of connection" with voters.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-48) The report also said that it would be difficult for Labour to win next time because of changes to constituency boundaries ([due in 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_periodic_review_of_Westminster_constituencies "2013 periodic review of Westminster constituencies")), voter registration changes and restrictions on trade union funding of parties. Beckett said the party should campaign in ordinary language, focus its policy on the condition of Britain in 2020, unite for the [2016 European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum"), and draw up a five-year media strategy.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Beckett_Report-47)

The Beckett report was criticised by some on the left wing of British politics as "show[ing] that many Labour politicians still don't really understand why they lost" and blaming factors such as the rise of the SNP on Labour's losses, rather than campaigning against [austerity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_government_austerity_programme "United Kingdom government austerity programme").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Socialist_Worker-49) Others criticised the report for being too broad and too vague in its conclusions. [Stephen Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Bush "Stephen Bush") wrote in the _New Statesman_ that "every bit of the Labour party will have something it can cling to" in the report:[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Stephen_Bush-50) He continued:

> Supporters of [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") will take heart from the fact that individual left-wing policies, like the mansion tax, were popular. But Corbyn-sceptics will note that it was voters that went for [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") and [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") that failed to back the party in 2015, which they will take as an endorsement of a centrist approach. Ed Miliband's diehard supporters – they do exist, believe it or not – will see the report as an endorsement of the Miliband era policy approach but will argue that a more convincing frontman would have sealed the deal.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Stephen_Bush-50)

[Owen Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Jones "Owen Jones"), a columnist for _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_, said that the left should not fear the Beckett report, saying: "Let's have a full inquest, not in the interests of navel-gazing, but in the interests of winning."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-51) According to the _[Morning Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morning\_Star\_(British\_newspaper) "Morning Star (British newspaper)")_, many centrist and more right-wing Labour politicians also welcomed the report.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-52) In Parliament, Beckett is Chair of the National Security Strategy (Joint Committee), and is a former member of the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament and Modernisation of the House of Commons Committee.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-53)

### National Executive Committee chairmanship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: National Executive Committee chairmanship")]

On 24 November 2020, Beckett was elected to succeed the [Transport Salaried Staffs' Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Salaried_Staffs'_Association "Transport Salaried Staffs' Association")'s Andi Fox as the Chair of the Labour Party's National Executive Committee. She was elected unopposed after NEC members from the left of the party staged a virtual walkout, protesting her election over then vice-chair Ian Murray from the [Fire Brigades Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Brigades_Union "Fire Brigades Union").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-54) Beckett was criticised after being overheard insulting a fellow NEC member during a [Zoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_(software) "Zoom (software)") call on 11 March 2021. Beckett thought her microphone was turned off when calling [Laura Pidcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Pidcock "Laura Pidcock") a "silly cow", after which Pidcock left the meeting.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Rodgers-55) Beckett apologised immediately and told the BBC the following day: "I deeply regret the remark, which was unjustifiable."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-BBC_12_March-56) Fellow NEC members called on her to resign, while Labour's general secretary [David Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Evans,_Baron_Evans_of_Sealand "David Evans, Baron Evans of Sealand") said that complaints against Beckett would be investigated.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-Rodgers-55)

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Honours")]

Beckett was appointed to the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_(United_Kingdom) "Privy Council (United Kingdom)") in 1993. She was appointed [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire") (DBE) in the [2013 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_New_Year_Honours "2013 New Year Honours") for public and political service[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-58) and was promoted to [Dame Grand Cross of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Grand_Cross_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Grand Cross of the Order of the British Empire") (GBE) in the [2024 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_New_Year_Honours "2024 New Year Honours") for parliamentary, political and public service.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-59) In November 2017, she was awarded the [honorary degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree") of [Doctor of the University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_the_University "Doctor of the University") (DUniv) from the [University of Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Derby "University of Derby").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-60) After standing down as an MP, Beckett was nominated for a [life peerage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_peer "Life peer") in the [2024 Dissolution Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Dissolution_Honours "2024 Dissolution Honours").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-61)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-62)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-63) She was created _Baroness Beckett, of Old Normanton in the City of Derby_, on 14 August 2024.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-64)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Beckett&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Personal life")]

She married the chairman of her local [Constituency Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Party "Constituency Labour Party"), Lionel "Leo" Beckett (born 1926), in August 1979.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-MargProf-13)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-LeoObit-66) Beckett employed her husband as her office manager, on a salary up to £30,000.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-67) The practice of MPs employing family members has been criticised by some sections of the media on the lines that it promotes [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-69) Although MPs who were first elected in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election") have been banned from employing family members, the restriction is not retroactive.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-70) Leo Beckett had two sons from a previous marriage, and three grandchildren. Beckett and her husband enjoyed caravan holidays [[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-71) throughout her political career.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-72) Leo Beckett died in 2021 at the age of 95.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Beckett#cite_note-73)
